content: A food allergy is an exaggerated immune system response that occurs when the body reacts to certain foods, such as eggs, peanuts, milk, or other specific substances, as though they are harmful. This reaction is mediated by the production of immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies and the release of histamine in response to the offending food. Symptoms of Food Allergy Symptoms of a food allergy typically appear immediately or within two hours of consuming the allergenic food. In rare cases, symptoms may develop several hours later. If symptoms occur shortly after eating a specific food, it is likely that a food allergy is present. Key symptoms include hives, a hoarse voice, and wheezing. Additional symptoms may include: Abdominal pain Diarrhea Difficulty swallowing Itching of the mouth, throat, eyes, skin, or other areas Lightheadedness or fainting Nasal congestion Nausea Runny nose Patches of itchy, scaly skin (atopic dermatitis), which may peel or blister Swelling (angioedema), particularly of the eyelids, face, lips, and tongue Shortness of breath Stomach cramps Vomiting In cases of oral allergy syndrome, symptoms may include: Itchy lips, tongue, and throat Swollen lips (in some cases) Causes of Food Allergy The immune system typically protects the body from harmful substances like bacteria, viruses, and toxins. However, in individuals with food allergies, the immune system mistakenly identifies certain foods as threats. This triggers the production of IgE antibodies and the release of histamine, leading to an allergic reaction. While food intolerances are more common, true food allergies are less frequent. Any food can potentially cause an allergic reaction, but certain foods are more commonly implicated. In children, the most frequent allergens include: Eggs Milk Peanuts Shellfish (e.g., shrimp, crab, lobster) Soy Tree nuts Wheat Food allergies often begin in childhood, but they can develop at any age. Many children outgrow allergies to milk, eggs, wheat, and soy by the age of five if these foods are avoided during early childhood. However, allergies to peanuts, tree nuts, and shellfish are typically lifelong. In older children and adults, common allergens include: Fish Peanuts Shellfish Tree nuts In rare cases, food additives such as dyes, thickeners, and preservatives may cause allergic or intolerance reactions. Additionally, certain fresh fruits and vegetables can trigger an allergy syndrome affecting the mouth and tongue due to their similarity to specific pollens. For example, melons contain substances similar to ragweed pollen, and apples have allergens similar to tree pollen. Although many people believe they have food allergies, fewer than 1% of the population has true food allergies. Most symptoms are caused by food intolerances, which are commonly associated with: Corn products Cow's milk and dairy products Wheat and other gluten-containing grains When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Immediate medical attention is required if a serious or systemic reaction occurs after consuming a food, particularly if symptoms include wheezing or difficulty breathing. If epinephrine has been prescribed for severe reactions, it should be administered as soon as possible, even before calling emergency services. Prompt administration of epinephrine improves outcomes. Anyone who has experienced an allergic reaction to food should be evaluated by an allergy specialist. Blood tests or skin tests can sometimes confirm the presence of a food allergy, but there are no universally accepted criteria for diagnosis. Elimination diets involve avoiding the suspected allergen until symptoms resolve, followed by reintroducing the food to observe for a reaction. Provocation (challenge) testing involves consuming a small amount of the suspected allergen under medical supervision. This test carries a risk of severe allergic reactions and should only be performed by a healthcare provider. Self-testing or deliberate reintroduction of allergens without medical supervision is strongly discouraged. Treatment Options The only definitive treatment for a food allergy is strict avoidance of the offending food. Other treatments, such as allergy shots and probiotics, have not been conclusively proven to be effective for food allergies. For infants with cow’s milk formula intolerance, a healthcare provider may recommend a soy-based formula or an elemental formula, if available. If symptoms are localized (e.g., a single hive on the chin after eating a specific food), treatment may not be necessary, as the symptoms often resolve quickly. Antihistamines can alleviate discomfort, and soothing skin creams may provide relief for skin symptoms. Anyone diagnosed with a food allergy should carry injectable epinephrine at all times and be trained in its use. If a serious or systemic reaction occurs, including widespread hives, epinephrine should be administered immediately, followed by transportation to the nearest emergency facility, preferably by ambulance. Outlook and Prognosis Avoiding the allergenic food is often straightforward if the food is uncommon or easily identifiable. However, individuals with food allergies may need to adopt significant dietary restrictions, carefully read ingredient labels, and inquire about food preparation methods when dining out. Possible Complications Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction that affects the entire body. Although oral allergy syndrome rarely leads to anaphylaxis, individuals with this condition should consult their doctor to determine whether they need to carry injectable epinephrine. Food allergies can also exacerbate other conditions, such as asthma and eczema. Prevention Breastfeeding may reduce the risk of developing allergies. Otherwise, there is no known method to prevent food allergies, apart from delaying the introduction of allergenic foods to infants until their gastrointestinal systems have matured. The appropriate timing for introducing specific foods varies between individuals. Once a food allergy has developed, strict avoidance of the allergenic food is the most effective way to prevent further reactions.
